Embodied Feeling and Inner Space

Michel Claeys《What is Essence Therapy》 · Ni Nanqi Translation

Method positioning of Essence Therapy

Michel Claeys defines Essence Therapy as a body-centered psychological counseling method that adopts the perspective of transpersonal psychology. In addition to listening and supporting, the counselor also guides the client into the inner process, identifies different inner spaces, and works with the experience that is present in the moment.

The "inner space" here mainly refers to two states: one carries injured feelings, memories and habitual reactions; the other can provide support, acceptance and choice, which is called resourceful inner space by Michel Claeys and is also often described as "inner parent".

Body feeling as a work entrance

A person can know why he or she is anxious but still be nervous in certain situations over and over again. Essence TherapyDo not regard “understanding the truth” as the end of your work. It invites attention: How do you feel in your chest, breath, shoulders, or belly when you talk about this now? How does this feeling change?

Being aware of bodily experience is the gateway to identifying the hurtful space. Afterwards, the counselor may guide the client to listen to relevant experiences, and may also help the client connect with a more powerful inner state. The age regression is one of those tools that is not required for every consultation.

resource inner space

Resources are not a slogan to comfort oneself, but the stability, care, confidence and ability to choose that people can actually experience. Michel Claeys believes that one of the keys to the work is to help the client gradually identify the injured state without equating it with "the whole me". Starting from a more resourceful state, people can respond to inner pain in new ways.

Integrate changes into daily life

An inner experience may lead to new understanding, but integration still requires concrete action: clarifying one's needs, deciding how to express them next time, or trying different responses in familiar relationships. Michel Claeys lists this link as the last step of the Seven Principles.
